Let E be a finite-dimensional real vector space.

Let f:E→GLR(E)f:E\to GL_{\mathbb{R}}(E)f:E→GLR​(E) be a function which is discontinuous everywhere.

I now want to give EEE a charted space structure in the following way: for e∈Ee\in Ee∈E I identify the open set EEE of my space-to-be-charted EEE with the open set EEE of my model space EEE using the linear map f(e)f(e)f(e). So these identifications are jumping around in a crazy way.

I now want to say that this charted space structure makes EEE into a differentiable manifold, because all transition maps are just the composite of two invertible linear maps so they're C∞.C^\infty.C∞.

Have I made a mathematical error here? I haven't thought properly about the definition of a manifold for nearly 40 years.

I am trying to supervise a student who is putting a Riemannian manifold structure on the nnn-sphere in an n+1n+1n+1-dimensional real inner product space, and to do this I'm trying to understand how we have made the nnn-sphere into a charted space. We seem to be using docs#stereographic' (in the root namespace?) which seems to me to say "given a point vvv in the nnn-sphere, project away from −v-v−v onto the nnn-dimensional space {v}⊥\{v\}^\perp{v}⊥; this gives a homeomorphism between vvv and a random nnn-dimensional inner product space which varies with vvv; now use docs#OrthonormalBasis.fromOrthogonalSpanSingleton to identify this random space with Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn; this uses the fact that a finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis, which is docs#stdOrthonormalBasis , which uses the axiom of choice. So what I'm suggesting above must presumably be true, and somehow I just was not expecting this at all!

Kevin Buzzard said:

I now want to say that this charted space structure makes EEE into a differentiable manifold, because all transition maps are just the composite of two invertible linear maps so they're C∞.C^\infty.C∞.

Yes, that's a perfect definition, both from the mathematical and the Lean point of view.

Wow, thanks! I suspect that we are very lucky that whoever did this chose to make the identification in an inner-product-preserving way, otherwise making the sphere into a Riemannian manifold would be far harder than expected.
I think that was Heather Macbeth IIRC

Why do you need charts to make the sphere into a Riemannian manifold?

I am trying to understand manifolds in Lean properly so I can teach them to a student. I don't know of any way to learn how manifolds work in Lean other than by ploughing through the code and working things out for myself. Last week I understood this ModelWithCorners thing and got as far as the definition of the tangent space of a point; this week in the meeting I understood how we created the tangent space of the sphere at a point under this convention that all tangent spaces should be equal to the model space despite the fact that in reality the tangent space of the n-sphere is a "moving" n-space. I am still not great on tangent bundles but there's always next week. One big breakthrough this week was that the variable named EB means "model space of the Base" not "model space of the Bundle". There is a lot of implicit knowledge here that users of this part of the library will know back to front but I don't know it and so I'm just reading the code and slowly working everything out from first principles.
Maybe one could use this opportunity to add a chapter on manifolds to MIL?
I think there should be a chapter on manifolds in MIL (and one in the Lean phrasebook also)! Writing on eis on my medium-term TODO list.
@Kevin Buzzard I'm very happy to take a list of things that tripped you up and include them there. Are you aware of https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib-phrasebook/pull/14 already?

Here's a question I don't know how to answer. Is the tangent bundle of a manifold itself a manifold in Lean? The reason it's hard to just figure it out with #synth is that I cannot guess the model space/model with corners.
The answer is yes: the total space of a C^n vector bundle is a C^n manifold, and the tangent bundle of a C^{n+1} manifold is a C^n manifold. Let me loogle for the declarations...
docs#TangentBundle.contMDiffVectorBundle is the second half, docs#Bundle.TotalSpace.isManifold the first half.
In general, I.tangent should be the model you want (where I is the model with corners on the base manifold).

I have been thinking about submanifolds and I hope this is the right thread to post my thoughts:

Ideally, one would show that the structure that @Kevin Buzzard isn't just a Riemannian manifold structure on the n-sphere SnS^nSn but compatible with the Riemannian manifold structure on the n+1n+1n+1-dimensional real inner product space. For example, by showing that the inclusion Sn⊂En+1S^n\subset\mathbb{E}^{n+1}Sn⊂En+1 is an isometric immersion. Here, I am just using Euclidean space En+1\mathbb{E}^{n+1}En+1 for concreteness.

However, the following seems more natural to me: show that Sn⊂En+1S^n\subset \mathbb{E}^{n+1}Sn⊂En+1 is submanifold and then use the induced Riemannian manifold structure.

That is, I would show that every point of $$S^n\subset\mathbb{E}^{n+1}$ has a neighborhood which is taking by a smooth map to the model embedding $$\mathbb{E}^n\subset \mathbb{E}^n\times\mathbb{E}^1$. This map is the product of above map by @Kevin Buzzard and ∣∣x∣∣−1||x||-1∣∣x∣∣−1. This means that SnS^nSn is a submanifold of En+1\mathbb{E}^{n+1}En+1.

And then I would develop abstract theory that every smooth submanifold inherits a Riemannian manifold structure by sending tangent vectors across the inclusion and evaluating the metric there. And for concreteness, I would compute the SnS^nSn distance function.

However, I couldn't find the notion of submanifold in mathlib.

I am fairly new to lean and mathlib and am looking for a small project I can contribute to mathlib. I am wondering whether formalizing the notion of submanifold and the fact that it inherits a Riemannian manifold structure could be it.

Any thoughts?

Hi @Matthias Goerner - funny how our paths are crossing again, twelve years after the Modern Math summer school in Bremen! I'm glad to hear you're interested to contribute to differential geometry and mathlib; we need more helping hands. Unfortunately, there situation is not as easy for beginners right now:

  • differential geometry has a steep learning curve
  • a number of basic prerequisites are "in progress" (so applications wanting to use these need to wait, or coordinate)
  • these prerequisites include the regular value theorem (which I'm supervising a master's thesis on), so many standard examples of manifolds are not so easy to rigorously prove yet

About your suggestions in particular:

  • mathlib knows about immersions and smooth embeddings (docs#Manifold.IsImmersion and docs#Manifold.IsSmoothEmbedding; these are predicates for a function f:M→Nf:M\to Nf:M→N to be an immersion resp. smooth embedding). The definition is the correct one in infinite dimensions (i.e., an immersion is locally a map of the form u↦(u,0)u\mapsto (u,0)u↦(u,0)). Proving the equivalence with the standard textbook definition (e.g., "injective differential" for immersions) is work in progress; #41796 has one direction and is waiting for review.
  • mathlib doesn't have isometries (of Riemannian manifolds) yet, but that's easy to add. I have written such code, @Théo Tyburn (supervised by me) is writing this down also.
  • submanifolds are indeed missing, but the right definition is harder to find. Since "M is a manifold" in Lean depends on a choice of docs#ModelWithCorners, you want "N is a submanifold of M" to also encode a relation between their models with corners. I have a candidate for this, and have been thinking about the right notion of submanifolds, but this hasn't converged yet. I can certainly share what I had, but I don't think it's a good first project.
  • the current definition of Riemannian manifold is not just "take a manifold, and then choose a Riemannian metric on it" (for technical reasons); instead the manifold and its metric go together. Changing the metric on a Riemannian manifold requires jumping through an extra hoop, which is doable (but again not too beginner-friendly). Thus, when N is a Riemannian manifold and f ⁣:M→Nf\colon M\to Nf:M→N is an immersion, "take the induced Riemannian metric on M" is a little tricky. I could mentor you through this, but I suggest you don't make this your first project.

Good news: I indeed see a good little project for you. Saying "f is an isometric immersion" is pretty doable already. So, you could prove that the inclusion of the sphere into its ambient space (either docs#EuclideanSpace, but any normed space should work) is both an isometry and an immersion. ("isometry" will depend on Kevin's student's work, so you'll want to coordinate; "immersion" does not.) I'm happy to mentor you here; just note that I'm on holiday next week (and my August is hectic, so I cannot promise instant replies).

An update of where we are in London: my understanding is that the current definition of "the manifold structure on a sphere" (docs#EuclideanSpace.instIsManifoldSphere) is the following.

1) Choose an n+1n+1n+1-dimensional real inner product space EEE, and define the nnn-sphere Sn(E)S^n(E)Sn(E) in EEE to be the vectors of norm 1.

2) Note that if vvv is a vector of norm 1 in EEE then it's not hard (using stereographic projection) to give a homeomorphism between the open neighbourhood Sn(E)−{−v}S^n(E)-\{-v\}Sn(E)−{−v} of vvv in Sn(E)S^n(E)Sn(E) and the hyperplane perpendicular to vvv in EEE.

3) Using Lean's version of the axiom of choice (which gives us a basis for every vector space, which we then apply orthonormalisation to) we can choose an arbitrary linear isometry between the hyperplane perpendicular to vvv in EEE and Rn.\mathbb{R}^n.Rn. We use these as charts for Sn(E)S^n(E)Sn(E), despite the fact that as vvv moves smoothly around Sn(E)S^n(E)Sn(E), these charts might be jumping around in a crazy discontinuous manner, a fact which none of the geometers seem remotely worried about but which surprised me (see the first post above).

We are now hoping that the way to put a Riemannian manifold structure on the sphere is by identifying the tangent space with Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn in this way and using the usual inner product on Rn.\mathbb{R}^n.Rn.

Patrick said

Why do you need charts to make the sphere into a Riemannian manifold?

and right now our answer is "we need tangent spaces, and isn't that how the tangent space is defined?" I can quite believe we're missing something.
how are you identifying the tangent spaces with R^n?

Kevin Buzzard said:

despite the fact that as vvv moves smoothly around Sn(E)S^n(E)Sn(E), these charts might be jumping around in a crazy discontinuous manner, a fact which none of the geometers seem remotely worried about but which surprised me (see the first post above).

It's usually not possible to make your charts vary continuously across the manifold, since doing so would trivialize the tangent bundle.

Aaron Liu said:

how are you identifying the tangent spaces with R^n?

According to this code here it's rfl (I mean -- I thought this was the point of the chart, I don't mean that I am going to use rfl in production code, in fact I still don't know what I'm going to use to identify the tangent space with E because we didn't get that far yet, we are likely to solve this today)

Kevin Buzzard said:

as vvv moves smoothly around Sn(E)S^n(E)Sn(E), these charts might be jumping around in a crazy discontinuous manner

I think a way to avoid this problem is not choosing a particular chart on Sn(E)−{−v}S^n(E)-\{-v\}Sn(E)−{−v}, but choose a chart and all other charts compatible with it and put them together. In this way somehow the family of charts varies continuously as v varies. I think some textbook prefers this way to define manifold.

Right -- one could define the atlas like this (the atlas could contain all isometries, not just a randomly-chosen one). But in fact the atlas for the sphere is just defined to be the union of the randomly-chosen charts. None of this matters, it means equality of manifolds is a bad concept but we knew this already (this is true for lots of reasons).

The correct way to put a Riemannian structure on the sphere is probably not to come back to the definition, and instead use the API (and, if it's not there, build it): the inclusion map from the sphere to the ambient space is an immersion, and there is an inner product on the tangent space to the ambient space, so it can be pulled back to an inner product on the tangent space to the sphere -- that's your Riemannian metric. The specific atlas used to put the manifold structure on the sphere, or the details of the construction, are just implementation details there.

It sounds like we really just want the theorem:

The pullback of a Riemannian metric by a smooth immersion is a Riemannian metric
